clinicalPearls: Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disorder, and the skin is affected in roughly a quarter of patients, sometimes as the presenting feature
Known as one of the great imitators, its lesions range from red-brown papules and plaques to nodules, and diascopy classically reveals an apple-jelly colour
Lupus pernio describes indurated violaceous plaques on the nose, cheeks and ears and is strongly associated with chronic disease and upper respiratory tract or pulmonary involvement
Scar sarcoidosis is the appearance of granulomatous infiltration within old scars or tattoos and should always raise suspicion of systemic disease
Erythema nodosum is a reactive, non-specific eruption that, with hilar lymphadenopathy and arthralgia (Lofgren syndrome), carries a favourable prognosis
Histology shows non-caseating epithelioid granulomata with sparse surrounding lymphocytes (naked granulomas), but infection must always be excluded
Because cutaneous signs may herald internal organ disease, every patient needs assessment for pulmonary, ophthalmic, cardiac and other systemic involvement

Treatment is directed at the underlying disease and ranges from potent topical or intralesional corticosteroids for limited skin disease to systemic corticosteroids and steroid-sparing agents for extensive or organ-threatening disease
reference.pathophysiology: Sarcoidosis is characterised by the formation of non-caseating epithelioid granulomata in affected tissues, thought to represent an exaggerated cell-mediated immune response to an as-yet-unidentified antigen in a genetically susceptible host. Activated CD4 T-helper lymphocytes and macrophages accumulate and organise into compact granulomata, driven by a T-helper-1 cytokine profile. In the skin this produces the varied papules, plaques and nodules seen clinically, while similar granulomata elsewhere account for the multisystem nature of the disease. The granulomata may resolve spontaneously or progress to fibrosis, and their tendency to arise within scars and foreign material reflects a localised granulomatous response to tissue disruption.
additionalDifferentials: Cutaneous tuberculosis and other mycobacterial infections
Granuloma annulare and other non-infective granulomatous dermatoses
Granulomatous rosacea and lupus miliaris disseminatus faciei on the face
Discoid lupus erythematosus and lupus vulgaris
additionalInvestigations: Skin biopsy demonstrating non-caseating granulomata, with stains and culture to exclude mycobacterial and fungal infection
Chest imaging to detect hilar lymphadenopathy and pulmonary infiltrates
Serum angiotensin-converting enzyme, calcium and inflammatory markers as adjunctive tests
Pulmonary function tests and, where indicated, cardiac assessment including electrocardiography
Ophthalmological review for uveitis and other ocular involvement
Serum and urinary calcium to detect dysregulated vitamin D metabolism
redFlags: Lupus pernio or extensive skin disease signalling chronic systemic sarcoidosis
Symptoms of cardiac involvement such as palpitations, syncope or conduction disturbance
Progressive breathlessness suggesting significant pulmonary disease
reference.prognosis: Outcome varies widely: acute presentations such as Lofgren syndrome and erythema nodosum often resolve spontaneously within months, whereas lupus pernio and infiltrative plaques tend to be chronic and may cause disfigurement, and prognosis ultimately depends on the extent and severity of internal organ involvement.
pitfalls: Assuming skin disease is isolated and failing to screen for potentially serious internal organ involvement
Diagnosing sarcoidosis without excluding tuberculosis and other granulomatous infections
Overlooking granulomatous change within scars or tattoos as a clue to the diagnosis
Missing asymptomatic cardiac or ocular disease that requires urgent treatment
